title: How Everyday Life Reflects the Message
overview: Paul tells Titus, his helper on the island of Crete, how different groups in the church should live, and grounds it all in God's kindness shown in Jesus.

parts.label: Teach what fits (v. 1)
parts.note: The verse opens by setting Titus against the false teachers of chapter 1, who spread empty stories. His teaching should be healthy and true, and it should shape how people actually live.

parts.label: Older men and women (vv. 2-3)
parts.note: Older men are to be steady, self-controlled and dignified, with faith, love and endurance that hold up over time. Older women are to avoid gossip and heavy drinking, and to pass on what is good to others.

parts.label: Younger women (vv. 4-5)
parts.note: Older women are to guide younger wives to love their families, manage the household and accept their husbands' authority, which matched the household expectations of the Roman world. The stated reason is reputation: so outsiders would have no grounds to speak badly of the faith.

parts.label: Young men and Titus himself (vv. 6-8)
parts.note: Titus, probably a young man himself, is to model the self-control he teaches, with honest motives and careful speech. The goal again is that critics find nothing to attack.

parts.label: Enslaved people (vv. 9-10)
parts.note: Enslaved believers are told to obey, not to argue back and not to steal, so their trustworthiness makes the message about God attractive. The letter treats slavery as a fact of life and does not challenge it, which many readers today find deeply troubling.

parts.label: Why: grace has appeared (vv. 11-15)
parts.note: The reason behind all this is that God's undeserved kindness has shown up in Jesus, offering rescue to every kind of person just listed and training them to live well while they wait for his return. Jesus gave himself to redeem, meaning to buy freedom for, a people of his own, and Titus is to teach these things with confidence and not let anyone look down on him.

disagreement: Christians differ on whether the instructions about wives submitting to husbands are lasting commands for today or, like the instructions to slaves, guidance shaped by that culture's household norms.
think: When people judge a set of beliefs by how its followers behave, is that a fair test or an unfair one?
